lessons.title: What Tailwind adds to CSS
lessons.summary: Use small classes to apply familiar CSS rules directly where you build the interface.
explanation: Use small classes to apply familiar CSS rules directly where you build the interface.

p-6 sets padding, text-xl sets a type size, and flex establishes a flex container. Tailwind generates CSS for classes found in the source. You still need HTML semantics, the box model, layout, and the cascade to explain the result. Start here after the HTML and CSS paths.
lessons.code:
Study desk

One useful task at a time
lessons.practice: Change p-6 to p-10 and text-2xl to text-3xl. Explain the two CSS responsibilities.
lessons.question: What does Tailwind do with p-6 found in your source?
options: Replace the HTML element with a React component
lessons.reason: Tailwind produces CSS utilities. It does not add interaction logic or change HTML semantics.
lessons.hint: Think about the layer that controls appearance.

lessons.title: Install Tailwind with Vite
lessons.summary: Connect the Tailwind Vite plugin and import the stylesheet into your app.
explanation: Connect the Tailwind Vite plugin and import the stylesheet into your app.

For a new vanilla app, create the Vite project, install its dependencies, then add tailwindcss and @tailwindcss/vite. Add tailwindcss() to the existing plugin list without removing other plugins. Import Tailwind in your CSS and load that CSS from the entry file. Run these commands in your own terminal; the lesson displays them as reference.
lessons.practice: Create the project locally and put text-3xl on a heading. Check the stylesheet import if the size does not change.
lessons.question: Which combination connects Tailwind to this Vite app?
options: Only adding class names without loading CSS
The Vite plugin plus the imported Tailwind stylesheet
Running the development server without installing dependencies
lessons.answer: The Vite plugin plus the imported Tailwind stylesheet
lessons.reason: The plugin compiles Tailwind and the stylesheet import brings its output into the page.
lessons.hint: Both compilation and CSS loading matter.

lessons.title: Use Tailwind with plain HTML and the CLI
lessons.summary: Compile a stylesheet with the CLI and link its output from your HTML.
explanation: Compile a stylesheet with the CLI and link its output from your HTML.

The v4 CLI lives in @tailwindcss/cli. Keep input and output as separate files. Watch mode rebuilds while you edit; a normal build writes the file once. This route is useful when you want plain HTML without a framework. The browser sandbox already provides Tailwind compilation for practice, so it cannot execute npm commands.
lessons.practice: Build the output locally, link it in HTML, then try watch mode while changing a utility.
lessons.question: Which file should the HTML link to in this CLI setup?
lessons.reason: The browser needs the compiled stylesheet. The input contains Tailwind directives that require compilation.
lessons.hint: Choose the file containing the generated CSS.

lessons.title: Install Tailwind in Next.js
lessons.summary: Use the PostCSS integration and load global CSS from the app layout.
explanation: Use the PostCSS integration and load global CSS from the app layout.

A newly scaffolded Next.js project may already include Tailwind; inspect its files before installing twice. For manual v4 setup, install tailwindcss, @tailwindcss/postcss, and postcss. Register the PostCSS plugin, import Tailwind in globals.css, and import that file from the root layout. Follow the React and Next.js foundations before building this project.
lessons.practice: Inspect a local Next.js project for its PostCSS config, CSS import, and root layout. Record which parts already exist.
lessons.question: Which plugin is used for a manual Tailwind v4 PostCSS setup?
lessons.reason: @tailwindcss/postcss integrates the compiler with PostCSS; the Vite plugin belongs to the Vite route.
lessons.hint: Match the integration to the build tool.

lessons.title: Understand Preflight and editor help
lessons.summary: Tailwind resets some browser defaults, so headings and borders need deliberate styling.
explanation: Tailwind resets some browser defaults, so headings and borders need deliberate styling.

Preflight is included in the main Tailwind import. It removes default heading sizes and margins and establishes predictable base rules. Add text and spacing utilities explicitly. An editor extension for Tailwind can help with completion and class previews, but it does not compile the stylesheet for you.
lessons.code:
Heading without size utilities

Deliberately styled heading

Border and padding are explicit
lessons.practice: Compare the two headings, then style the first with size and weight utilities. Inspect the border rule in your local browser.
lessons.question: Why can an h1 look like ordinary text after importing Tailwind?
options: It has lost its HTML heading semantics
Preflight resets default visual heading styles
lessons.answer: Preflight resets default visual heading styles
lessons.reason: Preflight affects appearance, while h1 retains heading semantics. Apply the intended type hierarchy explicitly.
lessons.hint: Separate semantics from browser styling.

lessons.title: Spacing, padding, margin, and gap
lessons.summary: Distinguish inner space, outer space, and space between children.
explanation: Distinguish inner space, outer space, and space between children.

p-6 adds padding on all sides, px-4 changes horizontal padding, and mt-4 adds top margin. gap-4 spaces flex or grid children. Numbered spacing follows the theme spacing token; keep a consistent rhythm.
lessons.code:
First

Second

Outside the group
lessons.practice: Change gap-4 to gap-8, then p-4 to p-8. Compare which space changes.
lessons.question: Which utility spaces the flex children?
lessons.reason: gap spaces children; padding is inside an element and margin is outside it.
lessons.hint: Locate the space between items.

lessons.title: Size elements without locking the page
lessons.summary: Combine flexible widths and readable maximum sizes.
explanation: Combine flexible widths and readable maximum sizes.

w-full fills available width, max-w-xl limits growth, and mx-auto centers a block when space allows. Fixed widths may overflow small parents. min-w-0 allows a flex child to shrink; min-h-dvh can establish a dynamic viewport minimum height.
lessons.code:
A readable width

This panel fills a small space and stops growing in a large one.
lessons.practice: Compare the narrow preview with w-full max-w-xl and with w-[700px].
lessons.question: Which pair fills small spaces while limiting the maximum width?
lessons.reason: A flexible width plus a maximum grows with its parent without requiring a fixed large width.
lessons.hint: Look for a width and a maximum.

lessons.title: Build a readable type hierarchy
lessons.summary: Use size, weight, line height, and line length to show what matters.
explanation: Use size, weight, line height, and line length to show what matters.

text-3xl controls size, font-semibold controls weight, and leading-relaxed controls line height. text-sm/6 combines size and line height. Preserve semantic heading order and readable contrast; tiny essential text is not a good way to solve a crowded layout.
lessons.code:
Learning notes

One clear idea

A short explanation deserves enough room to read. Size and spacing show how the parts belong together.
lessons.practice: Change heading weight and paragraph line height separately. Compare readability.
lessons.question: Which utility changes font weight?
lessons.reason: font-semibold changes weight; text utilities set size and leading utilities set line height.
lessons.hint: Separate weight from size.

lessons.title: Use color with a clear purpose
lessons.summary: Apply background, text, and alpha utilities without losing contrast.
explanation: Apply background, text, and alpha utilities without losing contrast.

bg-emerald-700 colors a surface and text-white colors text. bg-emerald-700/10 changes only that background alpha; opacity-50 affects the entire element and its children. A palette name does not guarantee contrast. Check the foreground/background pair and use text for meaningful status.
lessons.code:
Ready to study

Background alpha only

Whole element opacity
lessons.practice: Compare background alpha and whole-element opacity. Keep both examples readable.
lessons.question: Which utility changes only background alpha?
lessons.reason: The slash modifier changes the color utility alpha; opacity affects the composited element.
lessons.hint: Find the color-specific modifier.

lessons.title: Borders, radius, and shadows
lessons.summary: Use surface treatments to explain grouping and elevation.
explanation: Use surface treatments to explain grouping and elevation.

border sets width; choose an explicit border color. rounded-lg sets radius and shadow-sm adds a restrained shadow. Some v4 defaults differ from older tutorials. A container does not need every effect; use the treatment that clarifies its purpose.
lessons.code:
A grouped note

A lightly raised panel
lessons.practice: Compare a border-only group with a shadow-only group. Explain each purpose.
lessons.question: What accompanies border when its intended color matters?
lessons.reason: An explicit color avoids relying on an inherited border default.
lessons.hint: Width and color are separate choices.

lessons.title: Choose how elements participate in layout
lessons.summary: Use block, flex, grid, hidden, and invisible for their distinct purposes.
explanation: Use block, flex, grid, hidden, and invisible for their distinct purposes.

flex and grid establish container layouts. hidden removes an element from layout and accessibility exposure; invisible retains its space. sr-only hides text visually while preserving it for assistive technology. Do not interchange these when users still need the information.
lessons.code:
VisibleSpace remainsThird

An accessible description
lessons.practice: Change invisible to hidden and compare the occupied space.
lessons.question: Which utility removes the item and its layout space?
lessons.reason: hidden uses display: none; invisible keeps space and sr-only has an accessibility purpose.
lessons.hint: Think about display rather than visibility.

lessons.title: Align a row or column with Flexbox
lessons.summary: Choose the direction before aligning the main and cross axes.
explanation: Choose the direction before aligning the main and cross axes.

flex creates a row by default. justify-between distributes free space on the main axis and items-center aligns the cross axis. flex-col changes the axis directions. Prefer content-driven height and use gap for predictable spacing between controls.
lessons.code:
Today

Two tasks remaining
lessons.practice: Switch to flex-col and explain how the axes change.
lessons.question: In a default flex row, which utility aligns the cross axis?
lessons.reason: items-center controls align-items; justify-between works on the main axis.
lessons.hint: Identify the axis first.

lessons.title: Wrap controls and shrink long content
lessons.summary: Use wrapping and minimum-width rules for real text.
explanation: Use wrapping and minimum-width rules for real text.

flex-wrap allows another line. flex-1 takes remaining space, min-w-0 lets a flexible child shrink, and shrink-0 preserves a control’s size. truncate hides overflow on one line, so provide a way to read essential full content before choosing it.
lessons.code:
A_long_study_task_title_that_needs_to_fit_in_the_available_space

HTMLCSS foundationsBrowser interactions
lessons.practice: Remove and restore min-w-0 in the narrow preview with a long title.
lessons.question: Which utility removes the minimum-width obstacle for the flexible child?
lessons.reason: min-w-0 allows shrinking below the intrinsic minimum while flex-1 shares space.
lessons.hint: Inspect the minimum width.

lessons.title: Create grid tracks and child spans
lessons.summary: Define columns on the container and spans on its children.
explanation: Define columns on the container and spans on its children.

grid-cols-2 creates two equal columns; gap-4 spaces them and col-span-2 spans both. grid-cols-[1fr_2fr] creates unequal tracks. Keep a sensible DOM reading order: visual placement should not scramble keyboard navigation or the document meaning.
lessons.code:
Study topics

HTML
CSS
Both columns
lessons.practice: Change the track ratio and one child span, then compare the DOM order.
lessons.question: Where should grid-cols-2 be applied?
lessons.reason: The container defines tracks; child utilities control their placement within them.
lessons.hint: Find the element establishing the grid.

lessons.title: Position labels and manage overflow
lessons.summary: Choose a containing block and keep scrolling intentional.
explanation: Choose a containing block and keep scrolling intentional.

relative anchors an absolute child with top-3 right-3. sticky needs an inset such as top-0 and depends on the scroll ancestor. z-index stays within stacking contexts. overflow-hidden can clip text and focus; use overflow-x-auto for content that genuinely needs horizontal scrolling.
lessons.code:
New

CSS notes

A long code sample that needs its own horizontal scrolling area.
lessons.practice: Move the label with inset utilities and try the long line in a narrow preview.
lessons.question: What makes this article the positioning reference for the absolute label?
lessons.reason: The appropriate positioned ancestor supplies the absolute child’s containing block.
lessons.hint: Inspect the parent positioning rule.

lessons.title: Start responsive styling from the smallest layout
lessons.summary: Unprefixed utilities apply first; breakpoint variants extend them as space grows.
explanation: Unprefixed utilities apply first; breakpoint variants extend them as space grows.

grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-2 starts with one column and changes to two at md and above. sm is a minimum-width breakpoint, not a command for small phones. The default md begins at 48rem. Preview breakpoints use the iframe viewport, so a wide laptop does not automatically make a narrow preview match md.
lessons.code: <main class="grid grid-cols-1 gap-4 p-6 md:grid-cols-2"><article class="bg-emerald-100 p-4">First topic</article><article class="bg-slate-100 p-4">Second topic</article></main>
lessons.practice: Use wide and narrow previews and identify the base layout before the breakpoint.
lessons.question: What does md:grid-cols-2 mean with the default breakpoints?
lessons.reason: The md variant is a minimum-width condition; the unprefixed layout remains below it.
lessons.hint: Read the breakpoint as a minimum.

lessons.title: Target a breakpoint range
lessons.summary: Combine minimum and maximum variants when a rule should have a limited range.
explanation: Combine minimum and maximum variants when a rule should have a limited range.

md:max-lg:bg-emerald-100 applies from md until below lg. max-md targets widths below md. Keep a base rule that works outside the range. Custom breakpoint tokens should use consistent units so their generated order stays meaningful.
lessons.code:
A different background between md and lg

Emphasized below md
lessons.practice: Try max-md and md:max-lg locally at widths around their boundaries.
lessons.question: Which condition does md:max-lg represent?
options: At least md and below lg
lessons.answer: At least md and below lg
lessons.reason: Stacked variants combine their conditions, producing a bounded width range.
lessons.hint: Both conditions must hold.

lessons.title: Adapt a component with container queries
lessons.summary: Let a component react to its available parent space rather than only the viewport.
explanation: Let a component react to its available parent space rather than only the viewport.

Mark an ancestor with @container and use @sm: or @md: variants on descendants. Container breakpoints have their own scale, separate from viewport sm and md. This makes the same component usable in a sidebar and a main column. The queried descendant should have a query container ancestor.
lessons.code:
Narrow host

Study notes

Flexible host

Study notes
lessons.practice: Change the first host max-width and compare both copies in the same viewport.
lessons.question: What lets @sm:flex-row respond to each containing space?
lessons.reason: The container ancestor provides the inline-size context for its descendant query.
lessons.hint: Find the query container ancestor.

lessons.title: Use fluid values while preserving readability
lessons.summary: Let layout adapt without making content uncomfortably small.
explanation: Let layout adapt without making content uncomfortably small.

w-full max-w-3xl handles width without a fixed large size. An arbitrary clamp value can scale a heading between a minimum and maximum. text-wrap and line-length decisions remain important. Check real long content and zoom; a responsive screenshot alone does not show whether text is readable.
lessons.code:
A clear learning space

Keep meaningful content readable at narrow widths and larger text settings.
lessons.practice: Change the clamp minimum and test a long heading with browser zoom locally.
lessons.question: What does clamp provide here?
options: A preferred fluid size bounded by a minimum and maximum
A guarantee that all text fits at any zoom
lessons.answer: A preferred fluid size bounded by a minimum and maximum
lessons.reason: clamp bounds the preferred value; actual content and zoom still require review.
lessons.hint: Read the three size arguments.

lessons.title: Give media a stable frame
lessons.summary: Use aspect ratios and object-fit with descriptive alternatives.
explanation: Use aspect ratios and object-fit with descriptive alternatives.

aspect-video reserves a 16:9 ratio; object-cover fills the frame and may crop content. object-contain keeps the whole image visible with possible extra space. Set useful alt text and known image dimensions. Remote assets are blocked in this sandbox, so this exercise uses a local data image.
lessons.practice: Compare object-cover with object-contain and change the aspect ratio.
lessons.question: Which utility keeps the full image visible inside its frame?
lessons.reason: object-contain preserves the image within the box instead of cropping to fill it.
lessons.hint: Choose fit rather than crop.

lessons.title: Style hover and keyboard focus
lessons.summary: Give mouse and keyboard users clear interaction feedback.
explanation: Give mouse and keyboard users clear interaction feedback.

hover: changes appearance when a pointer can hover. focus-visible: helps show focus during keyboard navigation. Keep a visible outline or ring with enough contrast and offset. A hover color alone does not make a div behave like a button; retain native controls.
lessons.code: <main class="p-6"><button class="rounded bg-emerald-700 px-4 py-2 text-white hover:bg-emerald-800 focus-visible:outline-2 focus-visible:outline-offset-4 focus-visible:outline-emerald-700">Save notes</button></main>
lessons.practice: Hover, then Tab to the button. Compare both feedback states without removing focus.
lessons.question: What does focus-visible: styling help communicate?
options: That every mouse click saved data
lessons.reason: A visible focus treatment helps users locate the active keyboard control.
lessons.hint: Consider navigation without a mouse.

lessons.title: Style related elements with group and peer
lessons.summary: Respond to an ancestor or preceding sibling state without duplicating it.
explanation: Respond to an ancestor or preceding sibling state without duplicating it.

group marks an ancestor for group-hover or group-focus-within descendants. peer marks a preceding sibling for peer-checked or peer-invalid styling. Peer uses sibling relationships, so the marked element must come before the target. Neither marker creates state by itself.
lessons.code:
Study notes

Lesson details
lessons.practice: Toggle the checkbox, then move the span before the input and explain why peer styling stops matching.
lessons.question: Where must a peer-marked input be relative to the styled sibling?
lessons.reason: The peer variant follows a preceding-sibling relationship. DOM order matters.
lessons.hint: Inspect the sibling order.

lessons.title: Style forms and useful validation feedback
lessons.summary: Keep labels, invalid feedback, and disabled states understandable.
explanation: Keep labels, invalid feedback, and disabled states understandable.

Use native inputs with connected labels. invalid: can style a constraint-invalid field; peer-invalid can reveal nearby feedback. aria-describedby connects explanatory text. Styling disabled: changes appearance, while the disabled attribute controls behavior. Preview form submission remains local and blocked from the network.
lessons.code: Enter an email such as name@example.com.
lessons.practice: Type an invalid email, then a valid one. Check label focus and the disabled button.
lessons.question: What actually disables the button interaction?
lessons.reason: The attribute controls native behavior. Appearance alone cannot enforce a disabled state.
lessons.hint: Separate a style from a behavioral attribute.

lessons.title: Style data and ARIA states honestly
lessons.summary: Use state attributes as styling hooks while maintaining their real meaning.
explanation: Use state attributes as styling hooks while maintaining their real meaning.

data-[state=open]: responds to a data attribute. aria-expanded: responds to aria-expanded="true". Attributes do not implement a disclosure or tab widget; its behavior and keyboard contract still need to exist. Avoid setting ARIA only to get a color. This example uses a native details disclosure and its open variant.
lessons.code:
Status: ready

Read the study tip

Try one small change and inspect the result.
lessons.practice: Change the data-state value and use keyboard activation on the native disclosure.
lessons.question: Does adding aria-expanded="true" implement a working disclosure?
options: No; the actual behavior must match the attribute
Yes; it creates all event handlers automatically
Yes; it supplies keyboard navigation for any div
lessons.answer: No; the actual behavior must match the attribute
lessons.reason: ARIA communicates state rather than implementing behavior. It must describe the real interface.
lessons.hint: Think about semantics and events separately.

lessons.title: Use motion as feedback and respect preferences
lessons.summary: Animate relevant properties and provide a reduced-motion alternative.
explanation: Animate relevant properties and provide a reduced-motion alternative.

transition-colors avoids transitioning every property. duration-150 sets a short duration; motion-reduce:transition-none respects reduced-motion preferences. Transform utilities can move or scale elements without replacing layout rules. Keep essential feedback visible when motion is disabled.
lessons.code: <main class="p-6"><button class="rounded bg-emerald-700 px-4 py-2 text-white transition-colors duration-150 hover:bg-emerald-900 focus-visible:outline-2 focus-visible:outline-offset-4 motion-reduce:transition-none">Start a study session</button></main>
lessons.practice: Compare the hover transition with reduced motion enabled in your local system or browser tools.
lessons.question: Which variant targets a reduced-motion preference?
lessons.reason: motion-reduce applies when the user prefers less motion, so essential state feedback should still work.
lessons.hint: Find the preference-related variant.

lessons.title: Define design tokens with @theme
lessons.summary: A theme variable can create named utilities for your own visual system.
explanation: A theme variable can create named utilities for your own visual system.

In v4, @theme is CSS-first configuration. --color-brand creates color utilities such as bg-brand and text-brand. Other namespaces define font, spacing, radius, and breakpoints. Ordinary :root variables can hold data without creating utilities. The text/tailwindcss style block is a lab convenience: in a local app, put these directives in the input CSS after @import "tailwindcss". Keep tokens few and meaningful.
lessons.code: A shared identity
lessons.practice: Change --color-brand once and observe every brand utility.
lessons.question: Which directive defines a token that creates color utilities?
lessons.reason: @theme variables in recognized namespaces connect design tokens to generated utilities.
lessons.hint: Look for the theme configuration directive.

lessons.title: Use arbitrary values when a token is not enough
lessons.summary: Express an occasional custom value without turning every value into a one-off.
explanation: Express an occasional custom value without turning every value into a one-off.

w-[18rem] and grid-cols-[1fr_2fr] express arbitrary values. Underscores represent spaces where needed. CSS variable shorthand such as bg-(--panel-color) reads a custom property. Prefer a theme token for repeated values and reserve arbitrary values for a specific constraint.
lessons.code:
A specific constraint

The maximum width serves this content.
lessons.practice: Change the maximum width and the custom property independently. Explain which should become a reusable token.
lessons.question: When is a theme token preferable to repeating the same arbitrary value?
options: When the value represents a repeated design decision
When no element uses the value
Never; every utility must be arbitrary
lessons.answer: When the value represents a repeated design decision
lessons.reason: A named token centralizes a repeated decision and lets you change it consistently.
lessons.hint: Look for repeated meaning.

lessons.title: Build light and dark themes
lessons.summary: Choose system preference or a selector-driven dark variant deliberately.
explanation: Choose system preference or a selector-driven dark variant deliberately.

dark: follows prefers-color-scheme by default. For a manual selector, define @custom-variant dark with :where(.dark, .dark *). A theme toggle still requires actual JavaScript or application state, and persistence is a separate decision. Check surface, text, border, and focus contrast in both themes.
lessons.code:
Theme-aware notes

The text and surface change together.
lessons.practice: Remove and restore dark on the main element. Check both text and border contrast.
lessons.question: What does dark: use before you override its variant?
lessons.reason: The default dark variant uses system color-scheme preference; a selector override changes its activation.
lessons.hint: Distinguish the default from a manual selector.

lessons.title: Name a reusable state variant
lessons.summary: Use @custom-variant for a recurring selector condition.
explanation: Use @custom-variant for a recurring selector condition.

A custom variant can express a product state without repeating its full selector on every class. The selector must match real attributes or classes. Variant styling does not change those attributes, so state still belongs to the app. Keep the condition understandable for the next developer.
lessons.code: Ready for a short session
lessons.practice: Change data-study from ready to waiting and observe the variant condition.
lessons.question: Does defining @custom-variant automatically update application state?
options: Yes, it stores state in a database
No, it only defines a styling condition
lessons.answer: No, it only defines a styling condition
lessons.reason: The variant describes a selector condition; the application supplies the actual state.
lessons.hint: Separate styling from state updates.

lessons.title: Add a custom utility and use @apply carefully
lessons.summary: Extend CSS where the project needs it while keeping component responsibilities clear.
explanation: Extend CSS where the project needs it while keeping component responsibilities clear.

@utility registers a custom utility that can work with variants. @apply inlines existing utilities in a CSS rule. It does not create HTML, events, or a reusable component contract. Prefer component reuse when structure repeats; use CSS for a real shared styling rule.
lessons.code:
A shared frame

Custom CSS has a focused job.
lessons.practice: Modify the custom utility and compare it with the @apply rule. Explain which responsibility each covers.
lessons.question: What does @apply do?
options: Inline existing utility declarations into a CSS rule
lessons.answer: Inline existing utility declarations into a CSS rule
lessons.reason: @apply combines styling declarations; it cannot implement structure or behavior.
lessons.hint: Think in CSS declarations.

lessons.title: Add utilities to React components
lessons.summary: In React, Tailwind classes belong in className. The stylesheet still enters through your app entry.
explanation: In React, Tailwind classes belong in className. The stylesheet still enters through your app entry.
Keep the React plugin when adding the Tailwind Vite plugin. Import the CSS once in main.tsx. These files belong in a local React project; the HTML preview does not execute JSX.
lessons.practice: Move the card into a local React project and confirm its CSS import reaches main.tsx.
lessons.question: Which JSX attribute holds Tailwind utilities?
lessons.reason: React uses className for HTML classes; Tailwind handles the resulting class strings during the build.
lessons.hint: Think of the standard React attribute for a CSS class.

lessons.title: Map component variants to complete classes
lessons.summary: Keep each possible utility visible as a complete string when a component changes appearance.
explanation: Keep each possible utility visible as a complete string when a component changes appearance.

A map connects a small prop to known classes. Tailwind scans source as text, so constructing bg-${tone}-600 hides the final utility from detection. A complete class map is predictable and easier to review.
lessons.practice: Add a warning variant using complete utility strings instead of interpolated color names.
lessons.question: Which approach lets Tailwind find every variant?
options: A map with complete class strings
Build color names with string interpolation
Put a color name in an unrelated comment
lessons.answer: A map with complete class strings
lessons.reason: Detection needs complete utilities such as bg-emerald-700, not a template that only produces them at runtime.
lessons.hint: The build reads the file before your component runs.

lessons.title: Reuse structure without hiding the design
lessons.summary: Extract a component when several views share the same structure and behavior.
explanation: Extract a component when several views share the same structure and behavior.

Keep headings, spacing, and accessibility semantics close to the component. Use children for content and a small set of purposeful props. @apply can compose existing utilities in CSS, but it does not replace a component that owns behavior or markup.
lessons.practice: Extract two repeated cards into one component while keeping their headings and content meaningful.
lessons.question: What is a useful reason to extract this card?
options: Repeated structure with the same responsibility
Every element has more than two utilities
lessons.answer: Repeated structure with the same responsibility
lessons.reason: A reusable boundary follows repeated responsibility, rather than an arbitrary class-count limit.
lessons.hint: Look for something that changes together across views.

lessons.title: Resolve competing utilities deliberately
lessons.summary: Avoid competing utilities for the same property and state. Rearranging the class attribute is not a reliable fix.
explanation: Avoid competing utilities for the same property and state. Rearranging the class attribute is not a reliable fix.

CSS generation and cascade decide the winner, not the order of class names in HTML. p-4 and md:p-8 are purposeful responsive values; p-4 and p-8 on the same base state compete. Conditional maps help. Class helpers can join strings, and a compatible merge helper can resolve supported conflicts, but neither chooses your design intent.
lessons.practice: Remove one base padding conflict and explain whether the remaining breakpoint variant is intentional.
lessons.question: What decides which conflicting utility wins?
options: The CSS cascade and generated rule order
Always the last class in the HTML attribute
lessons.answer: The CSS cascade and generated rule order
lessons.reason: Class attribute order does not control CSS rule order. Choose a single intended value per state.
lessons.hint: Compare CSS rule order with HTML class order.

lessons.title: Use Tailwind across Next.js components
lessons.summary: Utility classes work in Server Components as well as Client Components.
explanation: Utility classes work in Server Components as well as Client Components.

A static card does not need use client just to have Tailwind styles. Add a client boundary when the component needs state, events, or browser APIs. Keep globals.css imported in the root layout and use the Next.js PostCSS setup from the installation lesson.
lessons.practice: Build a static Next.js page with utilities and identify one feature that would need a Client Component.
lessons.question: Does a static Tailwind-styled card need use client?
options: No, styling alone does not need it
Only if a color utility is used
lessons.answer: No, styling alone does not need it
lessons.reason: The client boundary follows interactive JavaScript needs, rather than CSS utility usage.
lessons.hint: Ask whether the component needs state or browser events.

lessons.title: Find out why a utility is missing
lessons.summary: Check the stylesheet connection before investigating source detection.
explanation: Check the stylesheet connection before investigating source detection.

Tailwind scans source text for complete class candidates and generates matching utilities. Ignored files, external packages, or runtime-built strings may not be scanned as expected. Inspect a known class first, then check the actual class string and file location.
lessons.practice: Investigate one missing background utility using the three diagnostic questions in order.
lessons.question: What should you check before changing scan sources?
options: Whether all classes can become inline styles
lessons.reason: If the stylesheet never reaches the page, source registration cannot fix the missing styles.
lessons.hint: Start at the connection between CSS and the page.

lessons.title: Register sources when automatic detection needs help
lessons.summary: Use @source for a real external location or a small explicit set of utilities.
explanation: Use @source for a real external location or a small explicit set of utilities.

Paths are relative to the stylesheet. Register an external UI package only if your app uses it. @source inline can generate specific utilities that do not appear in scanned files. Keep that list deliberate: generating every imaginable utility adds unnecessary CSS. Adjust the paths to your project rather than pasting an example blindly.
lessons.practice: Sketch the path from your stylesheet to an external component folder, then register only that source.
lessons.question: What does @source inline provide?
options: An explicit set of utility candidates
A replacement for loading the stylesheet
lessons.answer: An explicit set of utility candidates
lessons.reason: It tells Tailwind to generate the specified candidates during compilation, even if source files do not contain them.
lessons.hint: Distinguish class detection from stylesheet loading.

lessons.title: Share theme context with CSS modules
lessons.summary: A separately processed stylesheet may need @reference to understand your shared theme and utilities.
explanation: A separately processed stylesheet may need @reference to understand your shared theme and utilities.

@reference exposes another stylesheet to the compiler without emitting that stylesheet again. In a CSS module, reference your app stylesheet before @apply when it contains your theme or custom utilities. Keep layers in mind: ordinary unlayered CSS can override layered utility rules, so mix custom CSS intentionally.
lessons.practice: Explain why the CSS module references globals.css and where the app actually loads its global CSS.
lessons.question: Does @reference emit another full copy of the referenced stylesheet?
options: No, it shares compilation context without emitting that copy
Yes, it duplicates every style on every component
It runs the referenced file as JavaScript
lessons.answer: No, it shares compilation context without emitting that copy
lessons.reason: Reference provides theme and utility context for compilation. The global stylesheet still needs its normal import in the app.
lessons.hint: The name describes a reference, rather than a second stylesheet output.

lessons.title: Recognize a v3 tutorial before mixing its setup
lessons.summary: Tailwind v4 uses a different installation flow from many older v3 tutorials.
explanation: Tailwind v4 uses a different installation flow from many older v3 tutorials.

Use @import "tailwindcss" and the integration package for your build tool. Do not add the old init -p step to a fresh v4 setup. A migration of an existing v3 project needs the official upgrade guide, a supported browser target, and a review of changed utilities. For older browser requirements, choose a compatible version deliberately instead of assuming a newer setup fits.
lessons.practice: Inspect a tutorial date and commands, then identify which installation steps belong to v4.
lessons.question: Which stylesheet entry belongs to the fresh v4 setup taught here?
options: Run init -p for every new v4 project
Use no stylesheet entry at all
lessons.reason: The v4 integration starts from the CSS import and the correct build package. Migration is a separate task.
lessons.hint: Look at the installation lessons rather than commands from an older tutorial.

lessons.title: Ship generated CSS, not a browser compiler
lessons.summary: A deployed app should serve the CSS produced by its Tailwind build integration.
explanation: A deployed app should serve the CSS produced by its Tailwind build integration.

The interactive lab compiles locally so you can experiment. That is a learning environment, not your deployment recipe. In a real Vite or Next.js app, let the build generate CSS and check that the output loads. The Play CDN is for development. Avoid secrets in source and verify the real deployment after changing build configuration.
lessons.code:
# In a Vite or Next.js project with Tailwind already configured:
npm run build

# For a CLI project with src/input.css:
npx @tailwindcss/cli -i ./src/input.css -o ./dist/output.css --minify

# Your deployed HTML must load the generated stylesheet.
# The educational preview here does not run these terminal commands.
lessons.practice: Write a deployment checklist: build succeeds, CSS loads, intended classes appear, and the layout still works.
lessons.question: What should a production app serve for Tailwind styling?
options: Generated CSS from its build pipeline
A development browser compiler on every page
The npm install output as page content
lessons.answer: Generated CSS from its build pipeline
lessons.reason: Generating CSS during the build keeps the deployment aligned with the selected framework integration.
lessons.hint: Separate the lab experience from the files a real app deploys.

lessons.title: Build navigation that stays usable
lessons.summary: Start with real links, a clear brand, and a layout that can wrap on small screens.
explanation: Start with real links, a clear brand, and a layout that can wrap on small screens.

A responsive navigation does not need a pretend menu button. This example keeps every destination available with flex-wrap, visible keyboard focus, and distinct hover states. If you add a collapsible menu in a real app, implement its expanded state and keyboard behavior as well.

options: They point to sections that exist

lessons.answer: They point to sections that exist
lessons.reason: Navigation needs a real destination and usable labels, not only attractive utility classes.

lessons.title: Build a clear form with honest feedback
lessons.summary: Make labels, instructions, input states, and the submit action understandable before polishing the surface.
explanation: Make labels, instructions, input states, and the submit action understandable before polishing the surface.

Utilities style a form, but do not create persistence or server validation. Native required and email attributes help with basic input checks. This preview shows a local status message and sends nothing. A real application still needs appropriate server validation, success and error handling, and storage if it promises to save data.

lessons.practice: Add a labeled name field and keep the local-only status message accurate.
lessons.question: What do the utilities provide in this form?
options: A database and server validation automatically
A guarantee that submitted data is saved
lessons.reason: Form styling is separate from validation logic, network requests, and persistent storage.
lessons.hint: Read the demo message and look for a storage implementation.

lessons.title: Style task states with native controls
lessons.summary: Use a real checkbox to drive a task state instead of drawing a checkbox that cannot be used.
explanation: Use a real checkbox to drive a task state instead of drawing a checkbox that cannot be used.

Peer variants style a following sibling when the checkbox changes. The native control keeps keyboard support and an accessible label. details offers a simple disclosure without extra JavaScript. These states live in the current preview; saving tasks across visits would need a separate storage feature.

Why this practice matters

Layout and interaction both need deliberate choices.
lessons.practice: Add one long task label, check it, and confirm it wraps without pushing the checkbox out of view.
lessons.question: Which element should carry peer in this example?
options: The checkbox whose checked state drives the sibling style
A sibling placed after the text being styled
lessons.answer: The checkbox whose checked state drives the sibling style
lessons.reason: The stateful peer precedes the sibling targeted by peer-checked utilities.
lessons.hint: Follow the relationship from the input to the next span.

lessons.title: Compose a dashboard around real content
lessons.summary: Let a useful next action and readable content guide the layout instead of filling cards with invented metrics.
explanation: Let a useful next action and readable content guide the layout instead of filling cards with invented metrics.

This dashboard uses a sidebar at larger widths and a single column on small screens. min-w-0 keeps long content from forcing the grid wider. Every link targets a real section. The cards describe study tasks instead of pretending to track progress that the page does not store.

lessons.title: Bring the decisions together in a small page
lessons.summary: Build a responsive study page with a clear hierarchy, a reusable visual theme, and honest interaction states.
explanation: Build a responsive study page with a clear hierarchy, a reusable visual theme, and honest interaction states.

Use the lab to develop the layout, then move the markup into a local project using an installation path from the first module. Move @theme, @utility, and @custom-variant directives from lab style blocks into your input CSS after @import "tailwindcss". Review keyboard focus, long content, contrast, and narrow layouts. If you choose React or Next.js, keep the framework responsibilities separate from the Tailwind styling. The companion project gives you a review checklist rather than claiming a visual layout is automatically correct.
